# Solution Concept & Originality

**The domain constraint.** Advising customers on mobility subscriptions combines two requirements that are rarely served well by the same system: numerical precision in the recommendation, and clarity in its justification. These two requirements pull toward different technologies — deterministic computation and generative language — and our solution concept is essentially a proposal for how to combine them without letting either compromise the other. @fig-pipeline shows the resulting architecture and, in its colour coding, the division of labour that follows from this constraint.

![The four-stage pipeline runs inside the backend. Only the `forecast` and `advisor` stages involve the language model, and neither produces a monetary figure.](assets/pipeline-number-guard.png){#fig-pipeline width=100%}

**The combination and its rationale.** We combine a FastAPI/PostgreSQL service layer, deterministic pricing and scoring engines that carry the entire `analyze` stage, LangGraph for agent orchestration with persistent checkpointing, a university-hosted GPT endpoint (kiconnect.nrw) used in two clearly bounded places — demand reasoning in the `forecast` stage and the conversational Advisor — and Langfuse for prompt management and tracing. Each component is there to prevent a specific problem, not to complete a stack. LangGraph gives us durable conversation state across separate HTTP requests and the `interrupt()` primitive behind our confirmation gate; PostgreSQL serves as both domain store and agent checkpointer, removing a class of state-synchronization bugs; and Langfuse keeps prompts versioned and traceable rather than buried in source code.

**Our own contribution: the number guard.** The design decision that distinguishes this system from a standard retrieval-augmented assistant is a strict division of labor: the deterministic engines decide what is true, and the language model is only permitted to decide how it is said. In financial advice, a plausible-sounding but fabricated figure is worse than no figure at all, because it is indistinguishable from a correct one at the point of consumption. We therefore established the invariant that **the language model never produces a number that reaches the user**. Subscription comparisons, break-even calculations, CO~2~ estimates and forecast projections are computed in `agent/engines/`, and the model receives them as fixed context it may only narrate, contextualize or explain.

The forecaster illustrates this division most clearly, because it is the component where an LLM contribution is most tempting. The model *is* used there — but only to predict demand: it reads upcoming calendar entries and estimates how many trips per mode the customer will make, never what those trips cost. The predicted trip counts are then passed back through the same deterministic engine that produced the original figures (`attach_projected_category_analysis`), which converts them into euros. In short, the model changes what is expected to happen; the engine determines what it costs.

**Human oversight by construction.** The number guard governs what the model may say. A parallel constraint governs what it may do: no portfolio change is written to the database until the agent has paused on a LangGraph `interrupt()` and received an explicit user confirmation, so a mis-fired tool call cannot cancel a subscription on its own. This matters beyond engineering hygiene. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires that systems be designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them and intervene in their operation, and Article 50 requires that users be informed when they interact with an AI system. Our prototype is unlikely to be classified as high-risk, since recommending mobility subscriptions does not fall under the Annex III categories, but the interaction pattern it implements is precisely the one those provisions describe: the agent may propose and simulate any change, yet the irreversible step remains a human decision. Designing the gate into the control flow rather than into the prompt means the guarantee holds regardless of how the model behaves.

**From stated preference to computed weight.** A third element closes the loop back to the customer. The three onboarding priority sliders — cost, CO~2~ and flexibility — are resolved into normalized weights in `engines/scoring.py` and shared by both the within-category keep/switch/cancel decision and the cross-category modal-shift ranking. A stated preference is therefore not a cosmetic setting: it propagates into the arithmetic that produces every recommendation.

**Why this goes beyond a tutorial example.** The instructive property of this architecture is that its output can be checked. Because the engines are deterministic, their results are reproducible, unit-tested (119 tests) and usable as a reference; because the language model is confined to a narrow path, that path can be benchmarked against a naive single-call baseline (`agent/baseline_pipeline.py`) producing the same output schema. Tutorial agent systems typically give the model as much scope as possible. We did the opposite, examining each subtask for whether a language model was warranted at all — and for pricing, eligibility, scoring and projection the answer was no. That restraint is what makes the system measurable at all.
